                               Bangladesh: Country Profile
Official Name                       :   The People’s Republic of Bangladesh
State Language                      :   Bangla
                                        The first ten lines of the Song ‘Amar Sonar Bangla’
National Anthem                     :
                                        written by Nobel laureate Rabindranath Tagore
                                        Consists of a circle coloured red throughout its area,
                                        resting on a green rectangular background. The length to
National Flag                       :
                                        width ratio of the rectangle is 10:6 and the circle has a
                                        radius of one fifth of the length.
                                        The national flower ‘Shapla (Water Lily)’ (nymphea-
                                        nouchali) resting on water, having on each side an ear of
National Emblem                     :
                                        paddy and being surmounted by three connected leaves of
                                        jute with two stars on each side of the leaves.
Capital City                        :   Dhaka
Nationality                         :   Bangladeshi
Name of Currency                    :   Taka (BDT)
Independence Day                    :   26th March
Victory Day                         :   16th December
International Mother Language Day   :   21th February
Geographical Location               :   In South Asia between 20o 34 and 26o 38 latitude and
                                        between 880 01 & 920 41 east longitude.
Boundary                            :   North: India, West: India, South: Bay of Bengal, East:
                                        India and Myanmar.
Area                                :   56977 Sq. Miles or 1,47,570 Sq.Km
Territorial Water                   :   200 Nautical Miles
Population                          :   168.22 million; Male:84.19 and Female:84.03 Million
                                        (SVRS 2020, BBS)
Density                             :   1180 Per Square Km. (SVRS 2020, BBS)
Growth rate                         :   1.37 % (SVRS 2020, BBS)
Population Density per sq.km        :   1140 (SVRS 2020, BBS)
Literacy rate (7+)                  :   Both Sex-75.2% (SVRS 2020, BBS)
Literacy rate (15+)                 :   Both Sex-75.6, Male-78.2, Female-73.0, (SVRS 2020, BBS)
Per Capita Income                   :   US$ 2591
Religion based Population           :   Muslim -88.4%, Others-11.6% (SVRS 2020, BBS)
Administrative Units                :   8 Division, 64 District, 493 Upazila/Sub-distrct, 641 Police
                                        Thana , 4554 Union Parishad, 59990 Mouzas,87316
                                        Hamlets.(Source LGED)
Time                                :   GMT+6:00 Hours
Main Season’s                       :   Spring (February- March ), Summer (April-June),
                                        Monsoon: (July-September), Autumn (October-
                                        November), Winter (December-January).
Principal Rivers                    :   Padma, Meghna, Jamuna, Brahmaputra, Tista, Surma and
                                        Karnophuli, (Total 230 rivers including tributaries and
                                        branches.)
Best Tourist Season                 :   October to March

                                     Definition of terms
Enrolment: Number of Students officially enrolled in a given grade or level of education regardless
of age.

Class size: The average number of students together in a class enrolled.

Teacher Student Ratio (TSR): Refers to the proportion of teachers in relation to the number of
students in an institution. Calculated by dividing the total number of students in a school or group of
school by the total number of teachers them.

Urban Area: Refers to the area covered by municipalities, Upa-zila Head Quarters, District Head
Quarters and City Corporations in the country.

Cohort Survival Rate: Percentage of students enrolled at the beginning grade/year of the level of
education who reached the final grade/year at the end of the required number of year to the level of
education.

Dropout Rate: Refers to the percentage of students of any reason leave educational institutions (in
any given grade or level) and did not come back to finish the grade or level during that school years of
that level of education.

Completion Rate: The percentage of pupils/students in the beginning grade/year of the level of
education who finished or graduated from the final grade/year at the required number of years of that
level of education.

Gross Enrolment Ratio: Refers to the total enrolment of students in a grade or level of
education, regardless of age, expressed as percentage of the corresponding eligible official
age- group population in a given school year.

Net Enrolment Rate: Refers to the number of students enrolled in the official specific age
group expressed as a percentage of the total population in that age group.

School age Population: Population of the age group theoretically corresponding to a given
level of education as indicated by theoretical entrance age and duration e.g the population
from ages four ages to thirty inclusive regardless of the existing requirements of compulsory
education or the period of education provided for in various types of schools.

Co-efficient of Efficiency: It is a ratio of expected student years’ student years required to
complete the cycle by the graduates and the total years actually spent to produce those
graduates expressed in percentage terms. The ideal (optimal) number of pupil-years required
(i.e.in the absence of repetition and dropout) to produce a number of graduates from a given
school-cohort for secondary education expressed as a percentage of the actual number of
pupil-years spent to produce the same number of graduates.

This is a synthetic indicator of the internal efficiency of an educational system. It summarises
the consequences of repetition and dropout on the efficiency of the educational process in
producing graduates.

School Expectancy: The number of years a person of School entrance age can expect to
spend within the specified level of education.

Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs):


Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) are the universal commitment of the member states of United
Nations. To ensure peace and prosperities for the people of the planet by establishing partnership of all,
the 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) were designed to eradicate poverty and hunger by
ensuring protection of natural resources and climate for the future generation. Now the present context
of the world every country is surviving to achieve SDGs. Bangladesh is also committed to achieve
SDGs by inspiring its wonderful success in Millennium Development Goals




Education is the very much influential target of SDGs which is also the key instrument of development.
To ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities
for all, Goal 4 has been adopted aiming to attain 10 Global Targets. There are 12 Global Indicators as
well as 31 Thematic Indicators for the monitoring of quality education. Bangladesh has made
remarkable progress in improving access to education at all levels. It also gradually moving forward to
achieve the Sustainable Development Goal 4.

                                     Executive Summary


Introduction:
The education system of Bangladesh is comprised of mix of heterogeneous providers. A variety of
schools operate within the country; government run schools, privately run schools and madrasah,
English medium schools (British Curriculum), schools run by NGOs and kindergarten schools.
Primary education spans grade 1-5; Junior secondary grades 6-8, secondary grade 9-10, higher
secondary grade 11-12 and tertiary education grades 13 and above. It is noted that the government
is going to implement primary education comprising from grade I-VIII.

Bangladesh has a centralized Education system administered by the Ministry of Education (MOE)
with two divisions viz, Secondary and Higher Education Division (SHED) & Technical and
Madrasah Education Division (TMED) and the Ministry of Primary and Mass Education
(MOPME). The MOPME and DPE are responsible for planning and management of primary,
mass and pre-primary education. The MOE, DSHE and DTE are responsible for post-primary
education. The MOE and UGC look after the overall management of tertiary education.

Education is the pivotal tool of the development of any country. Given this view the incumbent
government has been giving top most importance to the expansion of education. For the past decade
Bangladesh has been investing more to achieve the education Millennium Development Goals
(MDGs). Besides reducing poverty, Bangladesh has made spectacular success in improving access to
education. The gross enrolment ratio in primary education in 2021 has reached 105.72% and net
enrolment rate 97.42%. The gross enrolment ratio in secondary education in 2021 reached 75.52%
while net enrolment rate 70.25%. Bangladesh has achieved gender parity for educational access in
both primary and secondary education (well in advance of their 2015 MDGs). Now disparity in favor
of girls student both primary and secondary level. The number of out of school children has been
continuously decreasing both in absolute and relative term. Bangladesh education system is large,
catering to over 40.34 million students (2021), involving many stakeholders (for example there are 14
types of providers in primary education, 11 examination broads at the secondary levels, about 96.74%
secondary education institutions are privately managed).

For the planning and development of the education sector, the ministries need a complete quality
database. With a view to up-dating the database, BANBEIS regularly conducts post-primary education
surveys. The base-line survey was conducted in 2008 after that the annual survey was conducted in
2009, 2010, 2011, 2012, 2013, 2014 ,2015, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019, 2020 and 2021. The purpose of
Bangladesh Education Survey is to provide up-dated educational information and key performance
indicators to the policy makers and other stakeholders. The scope of Annual Survey 2021 was very
broad. All the educational institutions imparting post-primary education were covered.
The present report based on Educational Survey 2021 data do not fully address issues such as
management, governance, equity and non-teaching staff. The socio-demographic characteristics of
students and teachers were not considered. One limitation of the survey is the difficulty in
obtaining data from English medium schools, Medical Colleges and Universities. The Annual
Education Survey 2021 has used 10 type questionnaires, one for each types of institution. The
questionnaires were presented to the Stakeholders Consultation Workshop and took feedback and
incorporated it before finalization. The questionnaires were also pretested before finalization.

Questionnaires were up-loaded to Website viz; www.banbeis.gov.bd to fill up and sent it to
BANBEIS server through On-line. The data collection started on 16.10.2021 and continued up to
31.10.2021. Editing was done at the field (USEO office) and head office to ensure quality of data.
Besides, Post Enumeration Check (PEC) was done for School, College and Madrasahs to
minimize errors. It was found that the main survey data were reliable and valid. According to the
Annual Survey 2021, there were 42648 Post Primary Educational institutions in the country.
Among them 36710 are unique Institutions holding EIIN, besides 5938 Institutions are attached to
other Institution. This number was 41981 in the year 2020.



Primary Education:
Annual Primary School Census (APSC) 2021 was conducted by The Directorate of Primary
Education (DPE) and the data shown in this report about primary education as secondary sources.

Bangladesh primary education (Preprimary to Grade V) system is very large, catering to 20.09
million students in 2021 through 25 types of providers. Among them the government primary
schools alone covered 13.47 million (67.09%) students. The total number of girl students was
9953252 (49.54%). The GPI 0.98 i.e., parity exists. In 2021 total teachers (GPS only) were
359095 with female teachers were 64.41% of all teachers. Variation was observed between types
of primary education institutions (Table 2.3)

Pre-primary education enrolment (Table-2.2) was 3125090 among them 1571608 (50.29%) were
girls. Drop-out was prevalent in every grade, the rate was higher in grade-4 3.92 (Table 2.23)

Gross Intake Rate (GIR) and Net Intake Rate (NIR) was 107.30% and 96.18% respectively (Table
2.13). A small difference was observed between boys and girls. Gross Enrolment Ratio (GER) and
Net Enrolment Rate (NER) in primary education have been increasing during the past decades.
GER was 107.7% in 2010 and reached 105.72% in 2021. GER of girls (106.14%) was higher than
that of boys. NER in primary education was 94.8% in 2010 and increased to 97.42% in
2021(Table 2.14). The growth was spectacular and confirms continuous increase of access of
school age children to education.
Drop-out rates have been continuously decreasing from 39.80% in 2010 to 14.15% in 2021(Table
2.24). Survival rates have shown a continuous growth trend from boys 65.90% and girls 68.60% in
2010 to boys 85.25% and girls 87.1% in 2021(Table 2.25).

As a result of increasing the growth of access, retention and survival of students the primary
education coefficient of efficiency rate has been increasing from 62.30% in 2010 and rose to
85.35% in 2021(Table 2.26).



Junior, Secondary and Higher Secondary Education:
Total institutions offering Junior and Secondary education were 20960 in 2021 including 666
upgraded government primary schools having student from grade VI to VIII. The number of
institutions in this sub-sector was 12012 in 1995, has been smoothly increasing. Side by Side the
enrolment and teachers also increased. In 2021, the total enrolment was 10.19 million among them
5.57 million (54.67%) were girls giving gender parity index near 1.21. The number of students per
institution was 473 in 2021. Total teachers were 266568 with 76832 female teachers. The
percentage of female teachers was 28.82 % in 2021 and 20.28 % in 2005. In 2021, the teacher-
student ratio (TSR) was 1:38 and the average number of teachers per institution was only 13.
Among all teachers 67.52% were trained. This percentage was 26.55% in Junior Schools 70.90%
in Secondary School and 72.13% in School & College (Table-3.4.4).

In the total institution in 2021 the share of Junior Secondary institutions was 11.18%, Secondary
institutions 78.87%, School and Colleges 6.77% and Upgraded Govt. Primary Schools 3.18%.
Among all institutions 20960, 96.74% were privately managed and only 3.26% was publicly
managed (Table-3.1.2). Rural-Urban distribution reveals that in 2021, 76.17% of institutions were
located in rural areas, 68.71% of teachers were working in the rural institutions, and 69.92 %
student was studying in the rural institution (Table 3.1.6).

The distribution by division reveals unequal distribution. As regards the number of institutions,
Sylhet had only 5.22% while Dhaka had 18.99 % of all institutions. As regards teacher the share
of Sylhet was 4.49% while Dhaka had 23.20%. As regards the enrolment, the share of Barishal
was 6.05% while Dhaka had 23.41% (Table 3.1.5).

The Annual Education Survey 2021 reveals that 98.42% of all institutions had electricity facility;
the percentage was 90.01% in junior Secondary Schools, 99.49% in Secondary Schools and
99.86% in School & College (Table-3.5.1). The number of institutions having multimedia was
77.58%. This percentage was 21.94% in Junior Schools, 84.04% in Secondary and 94.23% in
School & College (Table-3.5.2). Relatively more institutions have computer facility; 43.41% of
junior secondary, 92.69% of secondary, 97.75% of School & College, 87.36% of all institutions
(Table-3.5.3).
It is reported that 80.20% of all institutions have computer teacher though Computer education is
Compulsory for Secondary education. This percentage was 38.33% for Junior Schools, 85.39% for
secondary schools and 88.87% for School & College (Table 3.5.4). It is found that 82.65% of
institutions had internet facilities in 2021. It is also found that most of the institutions have safe
drinking water facilities 97.85% and about 96.35% institution have separate toilet for girls’
students (Table 3.5.6, 3.5.7 & 3.5.8).

College Education:
The institutions offering post higher secondary education are included in college education. The
following types are recognized as Intermediate Colleges, Degree (Pass) Colleges, Degree (Honors)
Colleges and Masters’s Colleges. The total institution involved in college education has been
increasing. The number was 3324 in 2010, 3475 in 2011, 3547 in 2012, 3793 in 2013, 3985 in
2014, 4113 in 2015, 4238 in 2016, 4419 in 2017, 4495 in 2018, 4551 in 2019, 4699 in 2020 and
4729 in 2021. Majority (85.45%) of college was privately managed and only 14.55% was
government managed (Table 4.1.1).

There are three types of colleges; one is co-education and one is exclusively for girls and the other
is exclusively for boys. In 2021, there were 769 colleges (16.26%) exclusively for girls. The
sharing of college by education type as, intermediate college (School & College and Higher
Secondary College) was 2788 (58.96%), Degree (Pass) 1048 (22.16%) and the remaining 893
(18.88%) were Degree (Honors) and master’s College. The total enrolment in 2021 was 4.737
million. Among them 2.386 million (50.37%) were girls. The gender parity index was 1.01 (Girls
to Boys). The share of intermediate colleges in total enrolment was 17.61%, degree (pass) 18.33%,
degree (honors) 29.17% and master’s college 34.89% (Table 4.1.4). In 2021, a college had on an
average 1002 students, the highest average number of students was 8346 in master’s colleges and
the lowest average number of students was 293 in higher secondary colleges (Table 4.1.5).

Total teachers in 4729 colleges were 137225. Among them 35551 (25.91%) were female and there
were small variations among all types of colleges (Table 4.1.4). The teacher-student ratio was
1:35, highest in master’s colleges (1:109) and the lowest in higher secondary colleges (1:16)
(Table 4.1.5).

The number of colleges, teachers and students was found to vary across divisions. The highest
percentage of college was in Dhaka division 1050 (22.20%) followed by Rajshahi division 780
(16.49%) and lowest in the Sylhet division 294 (6.22%) (Table 4.1.8). At the same time, the
highest number of students was in Dhaka division 1281954 (27.06%) followed by Chattogram
division 830871 (17.54%) and the lowest was in Barishal division 288123 (6.08%) (Table 4.1.8).
Rural and urban distributions reveal greater inequality. In overall distribution of students’
population, 73.88% live in urban areas and 26.12% live in rural areas. Education survey 2021
reveals that 53.61% of institutions are located in rural areas (Table 4.1.10).
Among all institutions 99.96 % had electricity, 89.64 % had multimedia facility (Table 4.5.1),
91.14 % had internet connectively (Table 4.5.3) and 40.11 % had solar panel (Table 4.5.2).



Madrasah Education:
Madrasah education is a subsector of education sector of Bangladesh. This subsector is also large,
catering to over 3.99 million students including Ebtedayee. This is popularly known as religious
stream quite distinct from general stream. The total institutions offering post-primary madrasah
education was 7820 in 2002, rose to 9291 in 2021. Ebtedayee madrasah offers primary equivalent
while post-primary madrasah covers Dakhil, Alim, Fazil and Kamil; which are equivalent to
Secondary, Higher Secondary, Degree and Masters Education of general stream.

In 2021 a total of 9291 madrasah offered Dakhil to kamil education. Madrasahs are absolutely
privately managed. Dakhil, Alim and Fazil are privately managed. Out of 259 Kamil madrasah
only 3 were Government managed madrasahs. Among 9291 madrasahs 9288 (99.97%) were
privately managed. Among 9291 madrasahs, 70.43% were Dakhil, 15.05% were Alim, 11.73%
were Fazil and 2.79% were Kamil. In 6544 Dakhil Madrasahs total students were 1400204; more
than 59.48% were girls. Average students per institution are 214. Total teachers were 110901 and
Total Student were 2657252; The average teachers and students per institution were 12 and 286.
Teacher-student ratio was 1:24.

There were 1398 Alim Madrasah with 460793 students and 20583 teachers. Girl’s students and
Female teachers were 55.46% and 17.87% respectively. Average students per institution were 330
and average teacher per institution is 15 persons. Teacher student ratio was 1:22. In 2021 total
Fazil madrasah was 1090 with 525597 students and 19544 teachers, girls’ students were 50.16%
Female teachers were 17.68%. Average student per institution was 482 and average teacher was 18
giving teacher-student ratios 1:27. There were 259 Kamil madrasah in 2021 with 270658 students
and 5973 teachers. Girls student were 33.42% of total enrolment. Female teachers were 18.75 %
of total. Average students per institution was 1045 and average teachers were 23, yielding teacher-
student ratio of 1:45 (Table 5.1.7).

The distribution of madrasahs by division reveals that 13.08% madrasahs were located in Dhaka,
17.74% in Chattogram, 16.26% in Rajshahi, 15.27% in Rangpur, 12.70% in Khulna, 12.51% in
Barishal, 4.31% in Sylhet and 8.14% in Mymenshingh (Table: 5.2.5). Rural-Urban distribution
shows that 85.94% of all madrasahs were located in rural areas. Variation between types of
madrasahs and the rural share was as follows: Dhakil 89.75%, Alim 82.83%, Fazil 78.35%, Kamil
38.61% (Table: 5.2.6). Most of the madrasahs 95.77% prepare annual development plan, 93.71%
conduct co-curriculur activities. About 66.90% madrasahs use computer for academic/pedagogy
purposes. Only 35.96% madrasahs have science laboratories and 12.51% madrasahs have Ramp
for special needs student. About 5.70% and 4.04% madrasah have introduced digital attendance
for teacher and student respectively (Table: 5.5.4).

Among all teachers only 26.63% teachers were trained. This percentage varies between 21.21% in
Kamil and 28.39% in Dakhil. Percentage of female trained teacher is 29.70% which is higher than
percentage of male trained teacher (Table 5.4.7).

Nearly 89.66% Heads of madrasahs are appointed while 10.34% are acting heads variation
between types of madrasahs was observed (Table 5.4.8).

Professional Education:
Professional Education includes 13 types of institutions. These are Medical University, Medical
College, Armed Forces & Army Medical College, Dental College & Dental Unit, Nursing and
Midwifery College & Institution, Homeopathic College, Unani/Ayurvedic, Textile Technology,
Leather Technology, Law and Art Colleges, Agriculture College, and Library Science in 2021,
there were 821 professional institutions in the country. This subsector has been growing. In 2000
total institutions were only 187. This number increased to 821 in 2021 (Table:6.2).

Among 821 institutions 15.71% were public and 84.29% were private. The rate of growth has seen
higher in private professional institutions. The total students in 13 types of institutions were
191409 in 2021 and 51789 in 2003, showing a continuous growth in the past. Among all students
62.72% were girls in 2021. The gender parity index was 1.68. The number of students per
institution was 233 in 2021, this number was 335 in public and 214 in private institutions. Among
all students, the percentage of students in medical college was 26.21%, 3.75% in Dental College
23.59% in Homeopathic College, 3.84% in Law college, 31.63% in Nursing College and 10.98%
in other 8 types of institutions.

In 2021, there were 17176 teachers. Among them, 7540 (43.90%) were female teachers. GPI was
significantly improved and stands on 0.78, the teacher-student ratio was 1:11. The percentage of
female teachers was different in different type of institution, lowest (13.64%) in Leather
Technology and highest (77.46%) in Nursing and Midwifery college. Division wise distribution
shows that 35.93% institutions were in Dhaka, 14.49% in Rajshahi, 12.42% in Chattogram,
10.23% in Khulna, 9.62% in Rangpur, 4.87% in Sylhet, 6.09% in Mymensingh and 6.33% in
Barishal.

Teacher Education:
Seven types of educational institutions comprise this sub-sector. These are: PTIs, TTC, TTTC,
VTTI Physical Education College, HSTTI and Bangladesh Madrasahs Teacher Training Institute
(BMTTI). This sector has been growing slowly. The total number of institutions was 129 in 2000,
143 in 2003, 215 in 2015 and 209 in 2021.
Among 209 institutions, 49.76% were government and 55.02% were privately managed. The
percentage by type of institution was: 49.76% was TTC, 32.02% PTIs 14.35% was Physical
Education College, and 3.83% were other institutions. About 23.44% were located in Dhaka
Division, 16.75% in Chittagong, 17.22% in Khulna, 15.31% in Rajshahi, 9.09% in Rangpur,
3.83% in Sylhet, 5.26% in Mymensingh and 9.09% in Barishal Division. This confirms uneven
distribution between divisions. There were only one TTTC, one VTTI and one MTTI in Dhaka
Division in the country.

Total trainee/students in 209 institutions were 33996 with an average of 163 per institution.
Among all students’, girls were 43.43%, GPI was 0.77. Percentage of girls was highest in PTIS
that is 64.00% and lowest 8.52% in TTTC. The average enrolment per institution was 173 in PTIs,
119 in TTCs, 458 in TTTC, 2416 in VTTI, 108 in Physical Education College, 254 in HSTTI and
2604 in BMTTI, showing large variation between types.

The Education Institution Annual Survey 2021 found 2952 teachers in 209 institutions, average 14
teachers per institution. Among all teachers 29.44% were female. These percentages show
variations between types of institutions. The gender parity index for all types of institution was
only 0.77. The teacher-student ratio was 1:12 in the teacher education sub-sector.

Technical and Vocational Education:
This subsector is diverse, catering to more than 1164880 students, involving many stakeholders
(for example 16 types of providers).Types of institutions involved were: Polytechnic, Technical
school and college, Glass and ceramic, Graphic Arts, Survey Institutes, TTC, Textile institutes,
Textile vocational, Agricultural training institute, Marine Technology, SSC Vocational
(independent) HSC Vocational/ BM (independent), Medical Technology, Medical Assistant
Training School (MATS), SSC Vocational (attached) and HSC business management (attached).
This is increasingly growing sub-sector: total institutions were 1416 in 2001, 2317 in 2003, 5790
in 2015, 6885 in 2018, 7259 in 2020 and 7761 in 2021. Total students were 131481 in 2001,
188686 in 2003, 872658 in 2015, 1067484 in 2018, 1118334 in 2020 and 1164880 in 2021. (Table
7.1)
Among the 7761 institutions, 38.33% were SSC Vocational, 43.28% were HSC BM/vocational,
5.66% were polytechnic, 2.90% were technical school and college, 2.72% were Medical Assistant
Training School (MATS) and 7.03% were other institutions (Table 7.3). Majority institutions
(91.26%) were privately managed and only 8.74% were publicly managed (Table 7.5). Division
wise distribution shows that 18.31% were located in Dhaka division, 22.88% in Rajshahi, 15.05%
in Rangpur, 15.05% in Khulna, 8.07% in Chattogram, 8.56% in Barishal and 2.51% in Sylhet
(Table 7.7).

Total enrolment in 7761 institutions was 1164880 with an average of 150 students per institution.
Total girls’ students were 316060 (27.13%) of total enrolment; the gender parity index was 0.37
(37%), much behind the national target of Equal or 100%. Both percentage of girls and gender
parity index were found to vary over long range among types of institutions (table 7.6).

Total teachers in the 7761 institutions were 54942 including 11269 (20.51%) female teachers. The
average teacher per institution was 7. The gender parity index was 0.25 (female to male). The
percentages of female teachers varied over a wide range among different types of institutions.
Teacher-student ratio was 1:21 for all types of institutions. This ratio was highest (1:116) in
Medical Technology Institutes and lowest (1:4) for Marine Technology.

University Education:
Annual Education Survey (AES) 2021 reveals that there were 160 Universities in Bangladesh, 50
(31%) were public and 110 (69%) were private. The total number of students was 1233529. The
average number of students per university was 7710, the average number of students in public
universities was 18030 and private University was 3018. Among all students, 36.30% were girls.
In Public University, this percentage was 38.71% and in private University this percentage was
29.74 %. The gender parity index was 0.57 in both public and private universities, 0.63 in public
and 0.42 in private universities.

Total teachers in 160 Universities were 30976. Among them only 29.33% were female. In public
University this percentage was 26.73% and in private University this percentage was 31.90%.
Variation was large among the universities. The average number of teachers in 2021was 309 in
public, 141 in private and 194 in both public and private universities. The teacher-student ratio
was 1:58 in public University, 1:22 in private and 1:40 in both public and private universities. The
number of teachers by designation shows that in 2021 there were 15426 teachers in public
Universities. Among them 29.35% were professors 17.22% were associate professors, 34.25%
were assistant professors and 17.32% were lecturers. Among the running public Universities, there
were no residential facilities in 8 universities. These are: National University, Bangladesh Open
University, Islamic Arabic University, Jagannath University, Rabindra University, Sheikh Hasina
University, Khulna Agricultural University, and Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman Aviation
and Aerospace University (BSMRAAU). Among the total teachers of private Universities, 12.26%
were professors 8.86% were associate professors, 23.56% were assistant professors and 53.51%
were lecturers.

The total students of 50 public Universities were 901509. Among them 105646 (12%) were
resident students and 88% were non-resident students. Among 105646 resident students only
42246 girls (40%) were resident students. As against 12% of girl students in the total girl students
in the public universities. This was the overall situation. University wise resident, non-resident
students of 50 Universities are given in Table 8.10. It is seen that percentage of resident students
varies over a wide range from 5% in Bangladesh University of Professionals to 100% in
Bangladesh Agricultural University and Patuakhali Science and Technology University. Only 43%
of all students were residents at the University of Dhaka.
[*Two International Universities are included in Private University section.]


Education Finance:
An account of education finance is given in chapter 9. The total national budget was Taka
2951000 million for 2015-2016, Tk.2843820 million for 2016-2017, Tk.3417930 million for
2017-18, Tk.3999560 million for 2018-19, Tk. 4201600 million for 2019-2020, TK.5389830
million for 2020-2021 and TK 6036810 million for 2021-2022. The share of Education in the
national budget was 11.78% in 2015-2016, 15.43% in 2016-2017, 14.25% in 2017-18, 13.52% in
2018-19, 15.03% in 2019-2020, 12.77% in 2020-2021 and 12.58% in 2021-2022. In 2015-2016,
2016-2017, 2017-2018, 2018-2019, 2019-2020, 2020-2021 and 2021-2022 the share of primary
was 4.91%, 7.79%, 6.44%, 5.62% ,5.72%, 4.63% and 4.36% while it was 6.87%, 7.64%, 7.81%,
7.9%, 9.31%, 7.45% and 8.14% for post primary. Though the Percentage share had been
decreased, the total allocation has increased with a big amount (Table 9.1).

Education recurrent expenditure was found to be Tk. 26656 crore in 2020-2021 and Tk 28672
crore in 2021-2022. It was found that around 12.11% of the total recurrent expenditure was
allocated under the head of Wages and Salaries in cash in 2021-2022 (Table 9.2 & 9.3). Per
student cost was estimated as Tk 19730
In 2020-2021 (Table 9.2)

(64.19%) are girls. The amount disbursed in this regard is Tk. 26064.8 million (Table-9.6). A big

Out-put Statistics:
The number of students appeared in SSC examination has been gradually increasing. Total
students appeared in SSC was 435918 in 1990, 756387 in 2004 and 694652 in 2019 and 1631308
in 2020 and 1792312 in 2021.The growth was more than 411% over the last 31 years; the growth
of girls was higher than that of boys, it was almost 622% within the last 31 years. Spectacular
growth occurred in the pass rate. Percentage of pass was 32% (30% girls) in 1990, rose to 94.08%
(94.88% girls) in 2021 (Table 10.7). The pass rate was higher in the science group 94.54% in 2020
and 96.03 in 2021 and lower in the Humanities group (Table 10.8).
Participation in vocational examination (SSC) and the percent of pass in examination showed a
continuously increasing trend. The percentage of pass was 68% in 1999 which was raised to
72.70% in 2020 and 88.49% in 2021. Girls’ performance was higher than that of boys, the passing
percentage of girls was, 76.67% in 2019 and 77.47% in 2020 and 88.48% in 2021 (Table 10.10).
Statistics on number appeared in HSC and percentage of pass reveals a continuous growth. The
number of students appeared in HSC examination increased in almost all the three streams.
Percentage of pass was 30% (31% girls) in 1990 which was increased to 71.85% (74.84%) in 2019
and in 2020 due to COVID-19 Pandemic the HSC & equivalent examinees were assessed based on
their previous public examination results and all were passed in HSC examination. In 2021, total
1115605 students participated in HSC examination, out of which 106242 students passed (545529
girls), the total pass rate was 95.57% (girls 96.67%) (Table 10.11). Participation in Dakhil, Alim,
Fazil and Kamil examination of madrasah streams and their pass rate showed a continuous growth.
The pass rate in Dakhil was 93.22%, in Alim was 95.49% in 2021 (Table 10.15).

Results of SSC and Dakhil graduates with grade point also reveals spectacular improvement over
time. In 2004 a total of 8597 got GPA 5 (A+) in SSC. This number increased to 162625 in 2021, the
growth was more than 18 times (Table 10.17). Similarly, in Dakhil GPA 5 score was obtained by
1288 in 2004, 6287 in 2019 and 7516 in 2020 and 14313 in 2021 (Table 10.19). A similar trend
was found in SSC (Vocational) and HSC graduates with grade points (Table: 10.20 and 10.21).
Results of Degree (Pass), Degree (Hon’s), Masters and Equivalent Examinations under the Public
Universities were shown in the table 10.25. The number of student’s appeared both in degree
(pass) and degree (hon’s) examination were increased from 2013 to 2020. The pass rate of degree
(pass) exam in 2013 was 76% in 2019 the rate decreased to 59% but the rate increased 70% in
2020. The same trend were found in Degree (hon’s) and Master’s result. But total number of
students in Higher education were significantly increased.

English medium School Education:
Annual Education Survey 2021 reveals that there are 137 English medium schools in Bangladesh.
Among them 30 are ‘O’ level, 90 are ‘A’ level and only 17 are Junior secondary level. Most of the
Schools are located in Dhaka Division (121) followed by Sylhet (7). The total number of students
in English medium schools are 68825, among them 30090 (43.72%) are girls’. The average
number of students per school is 502. Average students per school by levels are: ‘O’ level 247, ‘A’
level 651 and junior secondary level 164. Total teachers in English medium schools are 6453
among them 4671 (72.38%) are female. The average teachers per school are 28 in ‘O’ level, 59 in
‘A’ level and 17 in the junior secondary level. (Table:11.5)

Climate Change and Disaster Impacts on Educational Institutions:
There are a total of 9970 institutions found in specific Disaster prone areas. (like Surge cyclone,
flood, Salinity, water logging etc.) But additional 3214 institutions affects by any kind of disaster
and climate changes. Among them, 807 are Junior school including attached primary, 5030
Secondary Schools, 353 School& College, 880 College and 2900 Madrasahs. 23 institutions are
located in surge areas, 263 in cyclone, 1369 Institutions located in flood affected areas, 123 in
water logging, 3070 in salinity, 852 in River bank erosion 170 in Drought/Barind tracts, 211 in
Earthquake, 633 in Land slide from Hill and 3214 in other disaster prone areas. Survey data
reported that 559 (6.60%) institutions managed by government are located in different types of
disaster prone areas (Table 12.1).

Many hazard/losses found due to Climate change and disaster. Survey 2021 data reported that
about 20.25 % institutions did not able to recovery loss on building, 21.52% loss on furniture,
19.84% loss on door/windows, 5.45% loss on roof, 7.77% loss on water supply system, 11.76%
loss on sanitation facilities, 13.40% connecting road did not able to recover after last disaster
(Table 12.2).

Competency loss on Subjects of the students are categories in seven subjects such as; Bengali,
English, Mathematics, Science, Social science, Religion and others. There are three measurement
scales was consider about subject loss, these are-students can makeup at home, face massive
problems and irrecoverable or permanent loss. Survey data reported that student can make up their
subject loss in house as; 42.94% in Bengali, 58.36% in English, 57.94% in Mathematics, 57.58%
in Science, 38.68% in Social science and 34.65% in Religion subjects. On the other hand, student
face massive problem as, 39.29% in Bengali, 8.38% in English, 8.05% in Mathematics, 11.73 % in
Science, 45.37% in Social science, 51.54% in Religion subjects. But the irrecoverable/permanent
loss on subjects as, 17.77% in Bengali, 33.26% in English, 34.01% in Mathematics, 30.69% in
Science, 15.95% in Social science, 13.81% in Religion subjects (Table 12.5).

Initiatives taken by the institution for increasing capability of disaster impact recovery is as, no
notable initiatives taken by 12.42% institutions, problem identified and listed by 20.28%
institution, informed local administration with written by 15.77% institutions, put-up the problems
in various discussion by 16.76% and discussed in PTA & SMC meeting by 26.55% institutions
(Table 12.6). The situation about Evaluation report prepared and sent by the institution for long-
term disaster risk are- report sent as direction to the structured check list by 16.74% institutions,
evaluation report prepare but not structured way by 15.72% institutions, Institution Head informed
to the authority over phone by 30.38% institutions, report prepared only for institutions by 3.81%
institutions, never thought about this in 14.14 institutions and other 19.21% institutions reported
for preparing such kind of report (Table 12.7).

Performance Indicators:
In 2021, the gross enrolment ratio in the secondary level rose to 75.52% from 43.10% in 2001.The
gross enrolment ratio for boys in 2021 is 66.40%, significantly lower compared to GER for girls
83.15%. In 2021, the NER in secondary level was 70.25%, among them 63.29% for boys and
79.09% for girls. The gender parity index was 1.19. Significant improvement took place in
efficiency parameters. In 2021, the completion rate 64.93% among them 70.41% for boys and
60.56% for girls. The drop-out rate 35.07% in 2021 from 35.76% in 2020 (Table C5).

The Gross Enrolment Ratio (GER) in Higher Secondary level 48.79% among them 48.50% for
boys, 45.49% for girls’ which is significantly lower than boys. The Net Enrolment Ratio (NER) in
Higher Secondary level is found 40.54%, among them 41.88% for boys and 40.49% for girls’. The
GER and NER of the higher secondary level were 38.33% and 25.00% in 2008 but this rate has
increased to 2021.

The drop-out and completion rate at the higher secondary level (xi-xii grades) in 2021 are
presented in Table C6. The drop-out rate was 41.00% in 2000, reduced to 21.14% in 2021. The
completion rate reached to 78.86% among them 79.26% for boys and 78.44% for girls.

Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs):
At the secondary level (6-10), the gross enrolment ratio which is related to SDG indicator 4.3.1
(Participation rate in formal education) rose to 75.52 percent in 2021 from 72.78 percent in 2015.
The participation rate also progressed both in higher secondary (11-12) and tertiary level. In 2021,
the gender parity index (SDG indicator 4.5.1) for secondary level (6-10), higher secondary level
(11-12) and tertiary level were 1.21, 1.01 and 0.80 respectively; this was also significantly
increased and showing the high enrolment rate of girls in education against the boys in secondary
and higher secondary level. Data for SDG indicator 4.c.1 related to pedagogical trained teacher
show that 66.98 percent teachers at lower secondary and 60.84 percent teachers at upper secondary
level are trained; whereas, the female teachers about 67 percent and 74 percent are trained
respectively. The SDG indicator 4.a.1 related to facilities of schools show that 98.39 percent of
schools have electricity, 76.87 percent of schools have use the computer for pedagogical purposes,
97.48 percent of schools have safe drinking water, 96.62 percent of schools have single-sex basic
sanitation facilities that was really remarkable but only 18.76 percentage of schools having the
Ramp facility and 88.08 percent of schools having the basic hand washing facilities and 52.21
percent schools use the Internet for pedagogical purposes though 82.65 percent of schools having
the internet facilities. But the trend of progress from 2015 to 2021 in every respect were shown
significantly.
              Chapter – One
Introduction, objectives and survey methodology
                                     Chapter: One
                    Introduction, objectives and survey methodology
Introduction

Education plays key role in the development of any country. It is world-wide recognized that a
rapid improvement of education is end result for accelerating economic, social and human
development. The overall development can be achieved through proper and well-planned
education system catering to the diverse needs of the nation.

Considering the importance of education in building the nation all the governments in Bangladesh
regardless of their political character, affiliation and ideological learnings appeared to have
assigned a high priority to the expansion of access, equity and quality of education at all levels.
The present government also has taken different steps for the development of the education system
with the firm impression to build digital Bangladesh.

In order to achieve the goal of vision 2021, effective education planning and management are very
much essential. Updated, reliable and accurate data set is indispensable for the coherent
educational planning, development and management of educational system in Bangladesh. The
MOE is responsible for the planning and development of education sector. It is also responsible for
the effective and efficient management of the educational institutions of the country. To this end
the MOE entrusted the BANBEIS with the responsibility of providing valuable and authentic
information. The MOE asked the BANBEIS to follow scientific methods to establish facts and
figures for taking appropriate decisions.

With a view to providing accurate and up-dated data set for planning, development and
management of the education institutions as well as monitoring the progress (changes) of the
sector and sub-sectors, the BANBEIS starting from 2008 regularly conducted a survey of all
educational institutions involved in offering post-primary education. For primary education the
BANBEIS uses the data set regularly collected by the DPE through Annual Primary School
Census.

It is intended to collect through the education surveys all relevant data from all educational
institutions for knowing the parameters of important variables such as access, equity, quality,
continuation, drop-out, transition in relation to student’s participation, teaching and other facility
available in the respective institutions. The target population is enormously large. The number of
variables in each subsector is also big. The tasks involved are therefore gigantic and it not properly
executed, there are changes of non-sampling errors. The BANBEIS has been developing quality
assurance measures to minimize the non-sampling errors.
  The last education Census in the name of National Educational Survey (NES) was conducted in
  2008. Changes are continuously taking place. The number of institutions in each subsector, their
  enrolment, and teachers involved, facility is continuously changing. Many changes took places in
  the education sector. There have been spectacular increases in the number of institutions,
  enrolment and teachers all over the country. It is necessary to know whether equity and quality
  have been and maintained, whether girls are enjoying the fruits of expansion or disadvantaged
  tribes or social groups remain included as before. The existing database needs to be up-dated to
  meet the present day challenged facing the education sector. It is urgently felt the need for
  strengthening database at the BANBEIS. The BANBEIS has been conducting the survey regularly
  since 2008. The surveys 2009-2019 were conducted and the reports up to 2019 were published.
  The present report consisting statistical tables along with analysis in some cases.

  Aims and objectives of educational survey 2021

  The aims of the survey 2021 are;
  a. To collect up to date quality data for 2021 from all post primary education institutions to build
     a strong database and add the information of new institutions and delete the information of
     abolished institutions from the database.
  b. To develop skill of the BANBEIS professional in respect of conducting the surveys,
     monitoring, evaluation and research.
c.    To increase information awareness of teachers and administrators working in education with
      the data collected through the surveys and to simultaneously make both the data providers and
      users aware of the importance of facts and figures.
d.    To impart training to the teachers and administrators working in education for developing skill
      in filling up the questionnaires and also use of facts and figures.

  Specific objectives of the survey 2021

       The specific objectives of the Survey 2021 are;
  I.    To update existing database for post-primary education.
 II.    To publish Bangladesh education statistics 2021.
III.    To increase information awareness among all stake holders (teachers, managers,
        administrator, researchers and other users of information)
IV.     To make all information available to help Policy Makers, Education Managers and Education
        Researchers.
V.      To evolve methodology for assessing the efficiency of educational institution.
   Scope of the educational institution survey 2021.

   All the educational institutions imparting post primary education constitutes the population of this
   Survey. Every institution was the unit of measurement. Every upazila/thana was considered as
   enumeration area. Special attention has been accorded to cover all post-primary education
   institutions.

   Survey Methodology
   Appropriate methods and techniques were employed to conduct the survey. The following
   approaches were followed:

   1. Pre-survey activity
   The following important activities were undertaken to ensure the effective and efficient
   implementation of the survey:
a. In order to know what data were to be collected, BANBEIS conducted consultation
   workshops/seminars/meetings with the users and providers of data and shared their views. After
   getting feedback from workshop questionnaires were finalized;
b. After finalizing questionnaires, a on-line data entry software was developed and uploaded to
   BANBEIS website for data provide;



   2. Questionnaires: Drafting and finalization
   A total of ten questionnaires were developed for survey 2021 In view of the types and levels of
   education the following questionnaires were used for annual education survey 2021.

   (1) Unified Q-1 for school (2) Unified Q-2 for madrasah (3) Unified Q-3 for colleges (4) Unified
   Q-4 for school and colleges (5) Q-5 for Technical and vocational (6) Q-6 for professional
   Education and (7) Q-7 for Teachers Training colleges (8) Q-8 for public Universities (9) Q-9 for
   Private Universities and (10) Q-10 for English medium schools.
   These Questionnaires were sent to relevant offices for their opinions. Their comments were
   incorporated in these Questionnaires. The revised questionnaires were duly pre-tested. The valuable
   comments/observations obtained during pre-tests were considered during finalization of
   Questionnaires.

   3. Data collection, supervision, and monitoring
   BANBEIS has introduced e-survey for online data collection directly from the education
   institutions. After completing data entry and updating by the Institutions, it has been verified by
   the USEOs/assigned officers and submitted data in the central database of BANBEIS. Online data
   collection started on 16 October 2021 and continued up to 30 October 2021. The whole activities
   were supervised and monitored by field officials of BANBEIS and the Ministry of Education.
 4. Data quality control
 BANBEIS took all measures to ensure the quality of data. The following steps were undertaken to
 ensure quality.
    i. Post Enumeration Check (PEC)
    ii. Computerized data cleaning

 4.1 Post Enumeration Check (PEC)
      Post Enumeration Check (PEC) is a statistical practice to measure the extent of error incurred
      in the survey and thus adjust the data collected through 2021 survey. According to survey plan
      BANBEIS conducted post enumeration check to ensure quality and consistency of data. The
      PEC was carried out on a sample basis. The PEC covered school, college and madrasah.
      Detail’s description are shown in the annexure.

 4.2 Computerized data cleaning
      Data cleaning was done by using statistical package software like SPSS and STATA.

5. Data processing
Oracle based database software was developed, in-house with entry, edit and reporting models. The
entry form was developed using Php and Java while oracle 11g was used at the backend. Data
entry was made online directly from the institutions and post entry editing and cleaning was also
made before reporting.

6. Reporting
The initial job was to develop a tabulation plan. This was followed by generation of dummy tables.
The dummy tables formed the basic statement of the report. Finally, the dummy tables were linked
to datasets in the database and the data tables were created. The data tables were then edited to
give the present view. So the reporting flow was as follows:
Tabulation plan      dummy tables database         data tables   statistical tables report.

 7. Limitations

The Annual Education Survey 2021 covers 10 types of institutions located all over Bangladesh.
Record keeping of most institutions was found weak and unsystematic. So, data insert by the Heads
of institution was inadequate in some cases. Some Universities, Medical colleges and English
medium schools did not comply with BANBEIS request. The data for universities were taken from
the annual report 2021 published by BUGC and estimated data of medical and other institutions
were used while preparing this report.

Bangladesh Bureau of Educational Information and Statistics (BANBEIS)
                    Ministry of Education (MoE)




  Post Enumeration Check (PEC) Report 2021




          Statistics Division, BANBEIS, Dhaka, Bangladesh
Introduction
For the effective and efficient management and monitoring the progress of Education sector
BANBEIS regularly conducts an Annual Education Institution Survey (AEIS) of Post-
Primary Education levels. The AEIS collects data from all Post-Primary in 2021 there were
19540 Secondary Schools, 1420 School & Colleges, 3309 Colleges and 9291 Madrasahs.
AEIS data of 2021 gives a total view of Schools and Madrasahs. Among other the AEIS
collects data for knowing the parameters on important variables such as enrolment,
attendance, dropout, pass-rate, teachers, and training facility available at the institution level.
The target population in respect of each variable is enormously big. If data collection is not
properly done, there the chance of non-sampling error increases. These errors effect the
reliability and validity of the estimates. To improve reliability and validity of the survey data
BANBEIS regularly conducts validation sample Survey. The PEC is a standard practice
designed to know the extent of errors present in the AEIS data.
The PEC 2021 was designed to assess primarily the quality of AEIS data in relation to some
important variables such as enrolment, and repetition etc.

1.2. Objectives of 2021 PEC data
     The objectives are:
      To assess the quality of 2021 AEIS data
      To assess the level of accuracy of selected indicators
      To make necessary corrections of data of indicators through correction factor

1.3. Scope of Work
To achieve the objectives of the PEC 2021 it is necessary to collect relevant data through a
nationally representative sample of Schools and Madrasahs. For every sample school collect
data for each variable will be established. This data set will be compared with AEIS data set
to assess the level of accuracy of data set. The validation is expected to identify main factors
for incorrect recording and making AEIS data accurate.
1.4 Sample Size for the PEC 2021
Let n is the sample size for thevalidation sample Survey. We have two sets of data for the
same indicator, say enrolment of a class.
x1c x2c.......xncare n AEIS data x1s, x2s, ..... xns are n PEC data. We take x1s, x2s.........are n
correct data and xic is correct if xic, = xis otherwise xic has error incorrect.
For determining r, the Sample size, we consider the variable enrolment, the most important
variable.
In case the ith institutions is free from error then x1c = x1s
If all Schools are free from errors ∑ (X1c) =∑ (X1s)or

¯x1c=¯x1s, ¯Xc=¯Xs, Where ¯Xs and ¯Xc are population mean
If Pis the percentage of AEIS Schools with no error, Q= 1-P, n= Sample size then the
Standard formula for n is
n= (1.96)2pq×deff
      d2
≅768 for p=q=0.5, d=0.05 deff = 2
Thus a random Sample of 768 Institutions (Schools, School & Colleges, Colleges and
Madrasahs) would provide estimates at 5% level of significance with 95% confidence level.
1.5 Selection of Schools, School & Colleges, Colleges and Madrasahs
Random Sampling is used to select Sample Schools 471, School & Colleges 69, Colleges 84
and Madrasahs 193.

Data Analysis, Findings and Conclusions
2.1 Analysis plan
The AEIS data are available for all school, College and Madrasah. The BANBEIS provided
data for the schools, College and madrasah collected through AEIS 2021. The data set for
sample Schools is: x1c, x2c ….... xnc. The data collected through PEC are; x1s, x2s, ........, xns.
For ith institution the survey observation is xic and the survey observation is xis.
The difference xic-xis is the error for the ith school.
ei=x1c-x1s
=0 when x1c=x1s, positive if xic-x1s>0, -ve if x1c-x1s< o.
The survey data are free from errors if e1, e2, .... eN are all zero for all i. i.c
(X1c-X1s) is zero for all i-1, 2....N.

2.2 Total and average errors in the Sample.
ei= x1c-x1s, i =1, 2, ........n
∑n1 ei = ∑n1(x1c − x1s) = nxc − nxs = for the sample

𝑋𝑐 is the population mean for the survey data
𝑋𝑠 is the population mean for the validation set
𝑋𝑠 is the true mean of X1, X2, ......, XN
We propose and estimate of 𝑋𝑠 as follows.
                 𝑋𝑠
Estimate 𝑋𝑠 = 𝑋𝑐 𝑋𝑐, = 𝑋𝑐 (Correction factor= 1.00)
       𝑋𝑠

            𝑋𝑠
A, if CF=𝑋𝑐 =1, Survey estimate needs no Correction
CF > 1, Survey data provide under Estimate of the true value
CF < 1, Survey data provide over estimate of the true value

    (b) If।t।< 1.96, the survey estimate may be taken as true value, no adjustment is required.

   2.7 Conclusion and Recommendation
   For the indicators on enrolment, the relative difference between AEIS average and PEC
   average is found minimum. So, correction to the AEIS data is not required.

   The overall quality of AEIS 2021 data is good and up to the mark. To improve further,
   training of data management at the institution as well as central levels should be given more
   emphasis.

১.৬ িবন সংক্রান্ত

৩.১৩.২ সাংসে ক্ষটশলশভশদন প্রিাশরত শশখন-ক্ষশখাদনা কা িক্রদম আপনার শশক্ষা

       প্রশতষ্ঠাদনর শশক্ষাথীদের অাংশগ্রিণ ক্ষকমন?



৩.১৩.৩ আপনার প্রশতষ্ঠাদন স্বাস্থ্ুশবশি শনশিত কদর পাঠোন কা িক্রম পশরিালনা করা সম্ভব িদচ্ছ শক না?                                 িুাঁ-১               না-২
